# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure worldwide [1]. For decades, neurohormonal antagonism with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists formed the cornerstone of treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2]. The advent of angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) with sacubitril/valsartan represented a pivotal therapeutic advance, simultaneously augmenting beneficial natriuretic peptide signaling while suppressing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system [3].

## Mechanism of Action

Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [4]. Inhibition of neprilysin increases circulating natriuretic peptides, promoting natriuresis, diuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of pathological remodeling [5]. Because neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, neprilysin inhibition alone could paradoxically increase angiotensin II; thus, concurrent angiotensin receptor blockade with valsartan is essential [6]. Sacubitril is a prodrug that is converted to the active neprilysin inhibitor LBQ657 [7]. Earlier attempts to combine neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition (omapatrilat) were abandoned due to an unacceptable rate of angioedema attributed to dual bradykinin accumulation [8].

## Landmark Clinical Trials

The PARADIGM-HF trial fundamentally changed HFrEF management [9]. In this double-blind study, 8,442 patients with NYHA class II–IV HF and reduced ejection fraction were randomized to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril. The trial was stopped early for benefit: sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, reduced all-cause mortality, and improved symptoms [9,10]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and benefits across the spectrum of disease severity [11,12]. The drug was generally well tolerated, though hypotension was more frequent than with enalapril, while cough, hyperkalemia, and renal dysfunction were less common [9,13].

The TITRATION study provided guidance on initiation and uptitration strategies to improve tolerability [14]. In hospitalized patients, the PIONEER-HF trial demonstrated that in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan among patients with acute decompensated HFrEF was safe and produced greater reductions in NT-proBNP than enalapril [15]. The TRANSITION study similarly supported pre-discharge initiation [16].

In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the PARAGON-HF trial randomized 4,822 patients to sacubitril/valsartan or valsartan [17]. The primary composite of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death narrowly missed statistical significance (rate ratio 0.87; P=0.06) [17]. However, subgroup analyses suggested benefit among patients with ejection fractions below the median and among women [18,19]. These data informed regulatory labeling extending use to selected patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction [20].

## Biomarker and Imaging Effects

Sacubitril/valsartan increases BNP (a neprilysin substrate) while lowering NT-proBNP (not a substrate), an important consideration for biomarker interpretation [21]. The PROVE-HF study correlated reductions in NT-proBNP with reverse cardiac remodeling, including improvements in left ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, and left atrial size [22]. The EVALUATE-HF study demonstrated favorable effects on aortic stiffness and cardiac structure [23].

## Guidelines and Clinical Use

Contemporary guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association and the European Society of Cardiology recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational therapy for HFrEF, either replacing an ACE inhibitor/ARB or as initial therapy in newly diagnosed patients [24,25]. ARNI is now considered one of the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy alongside beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors [26]. Cost-effectiveness analyses have generally supported its value despite higher acquisition costs [27].

## Safety Considerations

Key safety issues include symptomatic hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal impairment, and angioedema [9,28]. A 36-hour washout period is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor to avoid overlapping bradykinin accumulation and angioedema risk [28]. The drug is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients with a history of angioedema [24]. Theoretical concerns regarding neprilysin inhibition and amyloid-beta accumulation have not been substantiated by available cognitive data, though long-term surveillance continues [29].

## Conclusion and Future Directions

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed HFrEF management, delivering robust reductions in mortality and hospitalization beyond conventional renin-angiotensin blockade. Its role in HFpEF remains nuanced, with greatest benefit at the lower end of the ejection fraction spectrum. Ongoing research is exploring early initiation, application in acute settings, and integration with newer agents to optimize comprehensive disease-modifying therapy [30]. ARNI stands as a landmark example of mechanistically rational drug development in cardiovascular medicine.
